* Ask for each request mark on its own, not both in one AND filter

GitHub's issues-list `labels` filter is conjunctive: a comma-separated list
selects the issues carrying EVERY name on it. `listMarkedIssues` passed both
marks at once, under a comment asserting the opposite, so it asked for issues
wearing both `task:origin:ad-hoc` and the retired `claude-task` — a set nothing
has ever been in. The list came back empty, adoption found nothing, and the run
reported success.

That has been true since #1138 replaced the single-label query with the pair, at
2026-08-21T09:58Z. The oldest un-adopted mark was filed four minutes later, and
25 requests have accumulated since, every one with `updated_at` still equal to
its `created_at`.

Each mark is now a listing of its own, unioned by issue number so an issue
wearing both spellings is adopted once rather than twice.

Nothing caught it because the adoption plan's tests hand `requests` in directly,
so no test ever exercised the read that produces them. The new file covers that
read against a fake that models GitHub's real conjunctive filter — a fake that
ORed would agree with the broken reader and prove nothing.

Refs #1354

* Fail the run on a work-item page that could not be read

`listWorkItems` broke its pagination loop on any non-200, which is the same
swallow the request listing just lost — a read that failed and a list that ended
were one outcome. Here the consequence is worse than a quiet no-op: the run
plans against the pages that did arrive, so a standing item whose page did not
reads as absent, and the run mints a second one beside it.

Refs #1354

* Bump claudinite-tasks to 60824.8

could not be read); planSchedulerRun gains the injectable async evaluate(task)
seam (fail-open on any read the scheduler cannot make - a missing
FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN, a failed signal, a throwing precondition), the board
watermark, the board-rewrite-on-change op and the retire-sleeping migration;
the executor's noGoPlan closes for standing and ad-hoc alike (rollBody stays

files an item only on a yes, records a no on the schedule board, and fails
open on any read it cannot make; the old 'pure function of the clock and the

re-ask, repo variable/cache/Project, orphan ref, closed board) and why the
board is not the slot run-ledger returned. §2/§6/§8/§9/§14/§16.4 move with it;

the machine-issue filter and the writing-tasks prose actually ship;

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run — and the queue's terminal labels rename (#1067)

* Queue labels: task:done/task:obsolete, and the origin marker retired

DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin
marker; the fielded engine still wrote the old vocabulary. This is the
engine-side half.

The terminals are `task:done` and `task:obsolete`, one namespace with the
state labels. Labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so the
read side accepts every retired spelling and maps it STRAIGHT to today's
in one pass: `terminalOfLabels` is the one decoder, and the old constants
stay exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads.

Standing versus ad-hoc is now derived rather than marked: the standing
item is the one titled with the task and nothing else, whose task is on a
calendar; a `manual` task's item and every qualified one are ad-hoc. The
occurrence guard, the dedupe, the `after` yield and the roll-vs-close
decision all read that instead of `origin:schedule`, which is no longer
written or ensured — only tolerated on items an older engine filed.

One behaviour follows from the derivation: an unqualified hand-created
item for a scheduled task WOULD be that task's standing item, so
`create-work-item` refuses it and names the two levers that do what the
operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`: label mechanics over the marked
issues, forming no judgment about who marked one. It consumes the mark and
every `claude-model:*` beside it, which is the whole exactly-once guard,
and it keeps one issue to one live item — a live prior run leaves the mark
waiting, a parked one is superseded.

The engine ships one task of its own, `engine/implement-request`, so a
request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker
would have performed is the precondition's.

The precondition IS the security check, at pickup. It refuses a request
nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses
one withdrawn or gone. A read that could not answer is NOT a refusal: it
fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

Two contract additions: the precondition takes the occurrence as a third
argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

Refs #1010

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Rebase onto #1071 and bump the growth pack for the contract prose

Refs #1010

* Ask for each request mark on its own, not both in one AND filter

GitHub's issues-list `labels` filter is conjunctive: a comma-separated list
selects the issues carrying EVERY name on it. `listMarkedIssues` passed both
marks at once, under a comment asserting the opposite, so it asked for issues
wearing both `task:origin:ad-hoc` and the retired `claude-task` — a set nothing
has ever been in. The list came back empty, adoption found nothing, and the run
reported success.

That has been true since #1138 replaced the single-label query with the pair, at
2026-08-21T09:58Z. The oldest un-adopted mark was filed four minutes later, and
25 requests have accumulated since, every one with `updated_at` still equal to
its `created_at`.

Each mark is now a listing of its own, unioned by issue number so an issue
wearing both spellings is adopted once rather than twice.

Nothing caught it because the adoption plan's tests hand `requests` in directly,
so no test ever exercised the read that produces them. The new file covers that
read against a fake that models GitHub's real conjunctive filter — a fake that
ORed would agree with the broken reader and prove nothing.

Refs #1354

* Fail the run on a work-item page that could not be read

`listWorkItems` broke its pagination loop on any non-200, which is the same
swallow the request listing just lost — a read that failed and a list that ended
were one outcome. Here the consequence is worse than a quiet no-op: the run
plans against the pages that did arrive, so a standing item whose page did not
reads as absent, and the run mints a second one beside it.

Refs #1354

* Bump claudinite-tasks to 60824.8

It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.

the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run — and the queue's terminal labels rename (#1067)

* Queue labels: task:done/task:obsolete, and the origin marker retired

DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin
marker; the fielded engine still wrote the old vocabulary. This is the
engine-side half.

The terminals are `task:done` and `task:obsolete`, one namespace with the
state labels. Labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so the
read side accepts every retired spelling and maps it STRAIGHT to today's
in one pass: `terminalOfLabels` is the one decoder, and the old constants
stay exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads.

Standing versus ad-hoc is now derived rather than marked: the standing
item is the one titled with the task and nothing else, whose task is on a
calendar; a `manual` task's item and every qualified one are ad-hoc. The
occurrence guard, the dedupe, the `after` yield and the roll-vs-close
decision all read that instead of `origin:schedule`, which is no longer
written or ensured — only tolerated on items an older engine filed.

One behaviour follows from the derivation: an unqualified hand-created
item for a scheduled task WOULD be that task's standing item, so
`create-work-item` refuses it and names the two levers that do what the
operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

Refs #1064

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`: label mechanics over the marked
issues, forming no judgment about who marked one. It consumes the mark and
every `claude-model:*` beside it, which is the whole exactly-once guard,
and it keeps one issue to one live item — a live prior run leaves the mark
waiting, a parked one is superseded.

The engine ships one task of its own, `engine/implement-request`, so a
request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker
would have performed is the precondition's.

The precondition IS the security check, at pickup. It refuses a request
nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses
one withdrawn or gone. A read that could not answer is NOT a refusal: it
fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

Two contract additions: the precondition takes the occurrence as a third
argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

Refs #1010

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Rebase onto #1071 and bump the growth pack for the contract prose

operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

Refs #1064

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`: label mechanics over the marked
issues, forming no judgment about who marked one. It consumes the mark and
every `claude-model:*` beside it, which is the whole exactly-once guard,
and it keeps one issue to one live item — a live prior run leaves the mark
waiting, a parked one is superseded.

The engine ships one task of its own, `engine/implement-request`, so a
request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker
would have performed is the precondition's.

The precondition IS the security check, at pickup. It refuses a request
nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses
one withdrawn or gone. A read that could not answer is NOT a refusal: it
fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

Two contract additions: the precondition takes the occurrence as a third
argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

Refs #1010

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Ask for each request mark on its own, not both in one AND filter

GitHub's issues-list `labels` filter is conjunctive: a comma-separated list
selects the issues carrying EVERY name on it. `listMarkedIssues` passed both
marks at once, under a comment asserting the opposite, so it asked for issues
wearing both `task:origin:ad-hoc` and the retired `claude-task` — a set nothing
has ever been in. The list came back empty, adoption found nothing, and the run
reported success.

That has been true since #1138 replaced the single-label query with the pair, at
2026-08-21T09:58Z. The oldest un-adopted mark was filed four minutes later, and
25 requests have accumulated since, every one with `updated_at` still equal to
its `created_at`.

Each mark is now a listing of its own, unioned by issue number so an issue
wearing both spellings is adopted once rather than twice.

Nothing caught it because the adoption plan's tests hand `requests` in directly,
so no test ever exercised the read that produces them. The new file covers that
read against a fake that models GitHub's real conjunctive filter — a fake that
ORed would agree with the broken reader and prove nothing.

Refs #1354

* Fail the run on a work-item page that could not be read

`listWorkItems` broke its pagination loop on any non-200, which is the same
swallow the request listing just lost — a read that failed and a list that ended
were one outcome. Here the consequence is worse than a quiet no-op: the run
plans against the pages that did arrive, so a standing item whose page did not
reads as absent, and the run mints a second one beside it.

Refs #1354

Refs #1354

**`main` on `main` is currently broken.** The first scheduler run after #1355 merged — [run 470](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32781936929) — died:

```
ReferenceError: parseBlockedBy is not defined
    at main (packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/scheduler-run.mjs:603:21)
```

`parseBlockedBy` has been used in `main` and never imported since the request lane was written. The line sits inside `for (const r of requests)`, and `requests` was always empty — so it never executed once across three days of green runs. #1355 made that list non-empty for the first time and the second bug surfaced immediately, hiding behind the first exactly as long as the first lasted.

I own this: #1355 is what put it in front of a runner.

## Why no test could reach it

Nothing drives `main` — its body is I/O against a live Action, so an identifier it names and never imports resolves at run time or not at all. There is no linter in this repo either, so an undefined name in an unexecuted path has nothing standing between it and production.

The blocker resolution is now an exported step, `blockersToResolve(items, requests, known)`, with both callers' rules unchanged — a blocked item's `Blocked-by` targets and a marked issue's, minus whatever `known` already answers. A test calls it, which is the whole of why the import can no longer go missing quietly. Verified see-it-fail: removing the import again turns those two tests red with the same `ReferenceError`.

## How it was caught

By forcing a scheduler run against the merged fix instead of waiting for the cron. That is the only reason this was three minutes of breakage rather than twelve hours.

## Verification

- Full suite **2742 pass, 0 fail**; `check_the_work` exit 0; `check_the_world` **0 blocking, 88 advisory** — unchanged.
- The 25 requests are still unadopted. The run that adopts them is the proof, and I'll force and watch it again once this lands.

